newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Qualified success for U.S. at trade conference.
newsitem.headline: Qualified success for U.S. at trade conference.

text.p: The United States did not get all it wanted on worker rights, but went away from the first World Trade Organisation meeting of ministers on Friday with a hard-won landmark deal to scrap tariffs on computer technology.

"All in all the United States is very pleased with the outcome of the first ministerial conference," Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky told a news conference at the end of the week-long meeting that was hosted by Singapore.

President Clinton called Barshefsky early on Friday morning to congratulate her on the Information Technology Agreement (ITA) to eliminate tariffs on hundreds of computer technology products by 2000. Information technology accounts for about $600 billion in world trade, of which the United States accounts for $90 billion, and is a major growth industry worldwide.

The agreement, signed by 28 countries with six more saying they intend to join, was an important diplomatic achievement for Clinton, who used his powers of persuasion at last month's meeting of Asian-Pacific leaders in Manila to win their support for the pact. Without that, Barshefsky told reporters, the agreement would never have come about.

But the ITA deal did not come without a price. The European Union, which had the most to lose because of its high tariffs on some computer products, pushed for and won concessions from the United States on product coverage and was able to wring from Washington an agreement to eliminate duties on liquor imports.
"Vive la France," said one U.S. delegate when asked by reporters why Washington made the concession.

The intense back-and-forth negotiations with European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan at one point prompted an outburst from Barshefsky questioning the EU's commitment to the agreement and to free trade.
The most contentious issue was labour rights. By law the United States was obligated to seek a WTO panel to examine worker rights and trade.
But in the face of fierce opposition by some Asian countries to any mention of labour in a WTO declaration, it was clear even before this week's meeting that that was not going to happen.
Barshefsky, though, found comfort in what she said was a growing appreciation at the WTO by countries of the issue of basic labour rights.
"As a practical matter, if working people don't believe these (trade) agreements are in their interest, politicians who are elected by working people won't be able to negotiate them," she said.

The United States was able to get a mention of labour rights into the final declaration, which also said that labour standards cannot be used as a protectionist weapon and that cheap labour in developing countries cannot be put into question.
The EU's Brittan described the statement as a "foot in the door" on the issue.
Agriculture was also a major concern for the United States and about 45 members of the 150-member U.S. delegation at Singapore were there to work on the agriculture issue.
The ministers agreed the WTO should lay the groundwork for a round of farm trade liberalisation negotiations that are set to begin in 1999.

The size of the U.S. delegation raised a few eyebrows at the conference. The delegation included members of Congress, private business representatives -- including those working the information technology issue -- union representatives and administration aides from the White House, Agriculture Department, State Department and U.S. Trade Representative's office.
